archetype.name: Game Manager (under-center efficiency)
archetype.definition: A low-aDOT distributor in a run-leaning, defense-first offense who has been asked to stay on schedule, feed his top receiver and avoid mistakes, and so far has done exactly that at a level far above anything in his past.

report.headline: A career-best two games, built on structure and Smith-Njigba, priced for regression
report.take:
Drew Lock has been a below-average NFL passer his whole career. Across five prior seasons his CPOE was negative every year, between -0.8 and -6.1. His best EPA per play was 0.104 as a 2019 rookie, and in 2020 his 15 interceptions ranked 62nd of 63. Through 48 attempts in 2026 he sits third of 42 qualifiers in EPA per dropback (0.451), second in adjusted net yards per dropback (10.5), and fourth in CPOE (6.72), with no interceptions and no turnover-worthy plays. That is not a modest improvement on a known player. It is a different player, over two games. The dossier is also murky on his role: the start log credits him with Weeks 2-4, the game log holds only two appearances, and the October 6 depth chart lists him as QB2. Anyone reading this card should first find out whether he is starting on Sunday.

The production has a clear shape. Seattle passes 5.1 points less than situation predicts (25th) and runs the ball poorly (26th in rush EPA), so Lock's job has been efficiency rather than volume. His intended air yards are 7.69, and he throws 1.25 yards short of the sticks on average. When the offense puts him under center he has been nearly perfect: 15 plays, 14-of-14, 0.891 EPA and an 80% success rate. Those are the scripted, defined reads a coaching staff builds for a backup. In shotgun, where the quarterback has to do more of the work himself, he drops to a 37% success rate and -2.5 CPOE, which looks a lot more like his career. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the other half of the story. He has drawn 21 of 48 targets at 1.178 EPA per target. Everyone else Lock has thrown to has been roughly ordinary, and Rashid Shaheed's 8 targets have lost value.

Several things inflate the headline numbers. Five deep attempts produced 1.971 EPA per play, and that is a handful of throws carrying the averages. The opponents were the 12th- and 27th-ranked defenses. The 31-7 rout of Arizona supplied most of his 22.5 total EPA. In the red zone he is 5-of-9 with a 33% success rate, which is thin. His bad-throw rate of 12.5% ranks 19th of 32. That is better than his career norm of 16-22%, but it is middling, and it is not the accuracy profile of a top-three passer. He also allows a 22.2% pressure-to-sack rate, close to what he has shown since 2021.

The structure is real: a top-three defense, short-game design and a receiver who wins. That gives Lock a playable floor whenever he is in. The 0.45 EPA level is not. A reasonable expectation for his starts is something like a slightly-above-average distributor, with the interception risk from his history still in the background, and that assumes he keeps the job. The backfield is also thinning: Jadarian Price is on IR and Zach Charbonnet is still on the PUP list. That leaves a weak run game even weaker, which tends to push more of the load onto the quarterback in exactly the shotgun situations where he has been ordinary.

strengths.title: Clean operation inside a structured script
strengths.body: Under center he has completed all 14 attempts at 0.891 EPA per play, and he has no turnover-worthy plays in 51 dropbacks. The staff has built him an offense of defined reads, and he has executed it without forcing anything. The approach is repeatable, but a perfect completion rate is not, and his 2020 tape says the interception floor has not disappeared.

strengths.title: Feeding Smith-Njigba early and often
strengths.body: Smith-Njigba has drawn 21 of his 48 targets and returned 1.178 EPA per target. When that player is open and the quarterback trusts him, the efficiency of the whole passing game follows. This should hold as long as both are on the field together, though defenses will start to tilt coverage toward him.

strengths.title: Short-area efficiency
strengths.body: Throws of 0-9 air yards have produced 0.524 EPA and a 59% success rate across 22 attempts. That is the core of what the offense asks of him. It fits a run-leaning team with an elite defense, where the quarterback is meant to move the chains rather than create explosives.

concerns.title: Two games against a career of evidence
concerns.body: His CPOE has been negative in every prior season, including -6.1 with the Giants in 2024, and he has never posted EPA per play above 0.104. Two games and 48 attempts, one of them against the 27th-ranked defense, are not enough to overwrite that. Expect heavy regression in both CPOE and EPA per dropback.

concerns.title: Shotgun looks like the old Lock
concerns.body: In shotgun he has a 37% success rate and -2.5 CPOE over 35 plays, a sharp gap from his under-center work. When the script runs out or the game requires dropback passing, his accuracy reverts to his career level. With Price on IR and Charbonnet still out, the offense may lean on shotgun more.

concerns.title: Role is listed as backup
concerns.body: The October 6 depth chart has him at QB2, and Sam Darnold started Week 1. The dossier does not say why, so his volume going forward is uncertain. That uncertainty matters more than any efficiency split.

trend.note: His passing EPA climbed from 6.4 against New England to 16.1 against Arizona, and his bad-throw rate fell from 18.2% to 7.7%. The opponent also dropped from the 12th-ranked defense to the 27th, which accounts for a good share of that rise.

nextGame.headline: Weak 49ers rush helps, but explosives will be scarce
nextGame.body:
San Francisco's defense is middle of the pack overall: 14th in EPA and 18th against the pass. Its pass rush is among the softest in the league, 27th in hit rate and 26th in sack rate. It is also 23rd on short throws, which is where Lock lives. The catch is that it ranks 2nd in explosive pass rate allowed and 4th in deep EPA. The handful of downfield shots that inflated his averages are less likely to land, and the game should come down to steady short gains rather than chunk plays. Quarterbacks have managed only 14.3 PPR points and 1.25 TDs per game against this unit.

Availability tilts toward Seattle's passing game. Nick Bosa (64% of snaps) and DT James Thompson Jr. are out, which removes pressure from an already weak rush. Starting safety Marques Sigle (88% of snaps) is doubtful with a high-ankle sprain, which loosens the back end. On Seattle's side, Price is on IR and Charbonnet will not be activated, so a 26th-ranked run game gets thinner. The bigger question is Lock himself, listed as QB2. On the other side of the ball, the 49ers bring the league's top offense (0.539 pass EPA) into a Seattle defense that ranks 3rd overall but 28th on short throws. Lock may need to keep pace in a game totaled at 47.5, higher than either of Seattle's earlier totals.

keyMatchups.title: Short game against a soft underneath defense
keyMatchups.body: Lock's 0-9 yard throws have produced 0.524 EPA, and San Francisco ranks 23rd defending short passes. With Bosa out and a pass rush already 26th in sack rate, he should get clean, quick looks. This is the matchup's real opening.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a stingy shell
keyMatchups.body: His 1.971 EPA on deep throws comes from 5 attempts, and SF allows the 2nd-lowest explosive pass rate. Sigle's absence is the one crack in that coverage. Without the deep hits, his yards per attempt should fall back toward 7.

keyMatchups.title: Can Seattle shorten the game?
keyMatchups.body: Seattle's formula is to run more than expected and lean on a top-three defense. With both lead backs out and SF ranked 1st in limiting explosive runs, that formula is harder to execute. If SF's 1st-ranked offense scores, Lock gets pushed into the shotgun dropbacks where he has struggled.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lock is under center at all, and if so, how much of the game Seattle can run from under center before the score forces him into the shotgun.

restOfSeason.body:
Everything depends on whether he holds the job, and the depth chart now lists him as the backup. When he does play, the framework holds up: a top-three defense keeps games close, the scheme keeps his throws short and defined, and Smith-Njigba gives him a reliable first read. That supports a respectable floor of roughly 200 yards with low turnover volume.

The current efficiency will not last. A 72.9% completion rate, 6.7 CPOE and 8.3% TD rate from a passer whose career CPOE has never been positive should drift toward a mid-60s completion rate and a TD rate around 4-5%. Interceptions will appear eventually. The thinning run game and tougher opponents, starting with San Francisco, will test the shotgun version of him, which so far looks like the one from his Denver and New York tape.
swingFactors: Seattle run game once Price and Charbonnet return
How much the offense stays under center

bets.reason: San Francisco allows 1.25 QB TDs per game (5th fewest), and Lock's red-zone success rate is just 33%. His 8.3% TD rate is the stat most likely to regress. Only applies if he is confirmed as the starter.

His YPA leans on 5 deep attempts worth 1.971 EPA each, and SF ranks 2nd in explosive pass rate and 4th in deep EPA allowed. Expect volume through short throws rather than chunk plays. Again, only if he starts.

Any market priced off his first two games is pricing a passer with a career-negative CPOE as a top-three quarterback. His shotgun numbers (37% success, -2.5 CPOE) are the more honest baseline against a better opponent.

confidence.note: 48 attempts, a QB2 depth-chart listing, and a career that contradicts the sample.
